options.a: UL (Underwriters Laboratories), which lists equipment
options.b: NFPA (National Fire Protection Association)
options.c: ICC (International Code Council), alongside the IRC
options.d: OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration)

distractorExplanations.a: UL tests and lists products to safety standards; it does not write or publish the National Electrical Code.
distractorExplanations.c: ICC publishes the IBC and IRC; the IRC electrical chapters are derived from the NEC, which NFPA publishes as NFPA 70.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA is a federal regulator that references consensus standards; NFPA publishes the NEC as NFPA 70.

options.a: Normal return path for unbalanced load current
options.b: Earth connection that limits voltage from lightning
options.c: Path that GFCIs depend on in order to trip on ground faults
options.d: Fault current path to clear overcurrent devices quickly

distractorExplanations.a: Carrying normal unbalanced current is the job of the grounded (neutral) conductor; the EGC carries current only during a fault.
distractorExplanations.b: Limiting lightning and surge voltage to earth is the role of the grounding electrode system, not the equipment grounding conductor.
distractorExplanations.c: A GFCI senses hot-neutral imbalance and works without an EGC (406.4(D) permits GFCI replacements on two-wire circuits).

options.a: Bathrooms and kitchen countertops only, per 210.12
options.b: Bedrooms, living rooms, and other habitable rooms per 210.12
options.c: Bathrooms, garages, outdoors, and other locations per 210.8
options.d: Locations within 6 ft of a sink, with dwelling garages exempt

distractorExplanations.a: 210.12 is the AFCI section, and 210.8 GFCI locations go well beyond bathrooms and countertops (garages, outdoors, basements, etc.).
distractorExplanations.b: Those habitable-room locations are the AFCI list in 210.12; GFCI locations come from 210.8.
distractorExplanations.d: The 6 ft sink rule is one 210.8 trigger, but dwelling garages are a required GFCI location, not an exemption.

options.a: People from shock by detecting 5 mA ground faults
options.b: Equipment from lightning and switching surges
options.c: Conductors from sustained overloads above their rating
options.d: Branch circuits from arc faults that can cause fires

distractorExplanations.a: Detecting about 5 mA of ground-fault current to protect people is the GFCI function, not AFCI arc detection.
distractorExplanations.b: Surge protection from lightning and switching transients is the job of an SPD (Article 242), not an AFCI.
distractorExplanations.c: Overload protection is the thermal trip of a standard breaker; an AFCI adds detection of arcing signatures.

options.a: Conductor volume in box does not exceed box capacity
options.b: Splices in the box stay within conductor ampacity limits
options.c: Raceway fill stays below 40% of the conduit area
options.d: Pull boxes are 8 times the largest raceway on straight pulls

distractorExplanations.b: Box fill is a volume calculation per 314.16; conductor ampacity comes from Table 310.16 and is unrelated to box size.
distractorExplanations.c: The 40% limit is conduit fill from Chapter 9 Table 1; boxes are sized by cubic-inch volume allowances in 314.16.
distractorExplanations.d: The 8× straight-pull rule is pull-box sizing in 314.28 for 4 AWG and larger, not the 314.16 box fill calculation.

options.a: Table 250.122, based on the overcurrent device rating
options.b: Table 310.16 (or applicable tables) with adjustments
options.c: Chapter 9, Table 8, based on conductor area and resistance
options.d: Table 220.12, based on the volt-ampere load per square foot

distractorExplanations.a: Table 250.122 sizes equipment grounding conductors by OCPD rating; conductor ampacity comes from Table 310.16.
distractorExplanations.c: Chapter 9 Table 8 lists conductor properties (area, resistance) used for voltage drop, not allowable ampacity.
distractorExplanations.d: Table 220.12 gives general lighting load per square foot for load calculations, not conductor ampacity.

options.a: Must be kept clear of foreign systems to 3 ft above the equipment
options.b: May contain ductwork within that zone if a drip pan protects the panel
options.c: Must be kept clear of foreign systems to 6 ft above or structural ceiling
options.d: Must be kept clear in commercial occupancies, with dwellings exempt

distractorExplanations.a: The dedicated electrical space extends 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower, not 3 ft.
distractorExplanations.b: Protected foreign systems are allowed only above the dedicated space; nothing foreign may occupy the dedicated zone itself.
distractorExplanations.d: 110.26(E) applies to indoor switchboards and panelboards in all occupancies, dwellings included.

options.a: One receptacle per wall section, plus one beside each doorway
options.b: Receptacles so no point along the countertop is more than 2 ft from one
options.c: One receptacle per room, with extra ones where the owner specifies
options.d: Receptacles so no point along floor line is more than 6 ft from a receptacle

distractorExplanations.a: 210.52(A) is a spacing rule (no floor-line point more than 6 ft from a receptacle), not a count per wall or doorway.
distractorExplanations.b: The 24 in. (2 ft) rule applies to kitchen countertop receptacles under 210.52(C), not general wall spacing.
distractorExplanations.c: 210.52 sets mandatory spacing for habitable rooms; a single receptacle per room does not meet the 6 ft floor-line rule.

options.a: Where 240.4(B) or specific exceptions allow next standard size up
options.b: Where 240.4(D) allows 12 AWG copper on a 25 A breaker
options.c: Where the load is continuous, permitting the OCPD at 125% of conductor ampacity
options.d: Where the next size up exceeds 800 A, per 240.4(C)

distractorExplanations.b: 240.4(D) does the opposite: it caps 12 AWG copper at 20 A overcurrent protection.
distractorExplanations.c: The 125% factor sizes the OCPD and conductors for continuous loads; it does not let the OCPD exceed conductor ampacity.
distractorExplanations.d: 240.4(C) removes the next-size-up allowance above 800 A; the conductor ampacity must then equal or exceed the OCPD rating.

options.a: Acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction for the installation
options.b: Evaluated by recognized testing lab for safety standard compliance
options.c: Bearing a label or symbol from the manufacturer showing its ratings
options.d: Recognized as suitable for a specific purpose, function, or environment

distractorExplanations.a: Acceptable to the AHJ is the Article 100 definition of 'Approved,' not 'Listed.'
distractorExplanations.c: Manufacturer markings are not a listing; 'Listed' means included on a list published by a recognized testing organization.
distractorExplanations.d: Suitability for a specific purpose or environment is the Article 100 definition of 'Identified,' not 'Listed.'

options.a: Utility transmission lines under exclusive utility control
options.b: Product safety standards for manufacturing electrical equipment
options.c: Installation of electrical conductors and equipment
options.d: Wiring of ships, railway rolling stock, and aircraft

distractorExplanations.a: 90.2(B) excludes installations under the exclusive control of an electric utility for generation and transmission.
distractorExplanations.b: Product construction standards are written by UL and similar bodies; the NEC covers installation.
distractorExplanations.d: Ships, railway rolling stock, aircraft, and automotive vehicles are listed exclusions in 90.2(B).

options.a: Damp locations such as basements with exposed foundation walls
options.b: Underground raceways, since the conduit keeps the cable dry
options.c: Exposed in commercial parking garages if run along the ceiling joists
options.d: Dry, protected locations per 334 (typically not wet or exposed)

distractorExplanations.a: NM-B is limited to dry locations; damp or wet locations call for NMC-type or UF cable or another listed method.
distractorExplanations.b: Underground raceways are wet locations per 300.5(B), so NM-B is not permitted inside them.
distractorExplanations.c: 334.12 restricts NM where exposed to physical damage and in certain occupancies; exposed garage runs need another wiring method.

options.a: Table 310.16 ampacity, since fill depends on conductor heat
options.b: Box fill volume in 314.16 for each conductor size
options.c: Chapter 9 Table 1 and conductor fill (often about 9 for 40% fill)
options.d: Chapter 9 Table 8 conductor area alone, with no percentage limit

distractorExplanations.a: Ampacity tables set current ratings; the number of conductors in a raceway comes from Chapter 9 fill percentages.
distractorExplanations.b: 314.16 sizes boxes by cubic-inch allowances; raceway fill uses Chapter 9 Table 1 and Tables 4 and 5.
distractorExplanations.d: Table 8 gives bare conductor properties; fill uses insulated areas from Table 5 against the Table 1 percentage limit.

options.a: Three locations, one for each terminal on the switch
options.b: Two locations using traveler conductors between switches
options.c: Two locations, using a shared neutral between the switches
options.d: One location, switching three separate loads independently

distractorExplanations.a: Three terminals (common plus two travelers) serve two locations; a third location requires a four-way switch.
distractorExplanations.c: The conductors between three-way switches are travelers, which are ungrounded conductors, not neutrals.
distractorExplanations.d: Three-way refers to the switch's three terminals for two-location control, not to switching three loads.

options.a: Has an internal aluminum bonding strip in contact with the armor so the armor serves as the EGC
options.b: Is limited to dry locations and cannot be installed in wet locations
options.c: Uses full size aluminum interlocked armor as EGC (typical) without separate thin strip
options.d: Is permitted in exposed runs and not concealed in walls

distractorExplanations.a: The internal bonding strip that lets the armor serve as the EGC is the defining feature of Type AC cable, not MC.
distractorExplanations.b: MC cable with a listed jacket is permitted in wet locations; dry-location limits apply to other cable types such as NM.
distractorExplanations.d: MC cable may be installed exposed or concealed under 330.10; there is no ban on concealed runs.

options.a: 314.16 based on conductor volume allowances per AWG size
options.b: 314.28 at 6 times the largest raceway trade size for straight pulls
options.c: Chapter 9 Table 1 based on 40% fill of the largest conduit
options.d: 314.28 based on conduit trade size and number of bends/conductors

distractorExplanations.a: 314.16 box fill applies to conductors 6 AWG and smaller; boxes for 4 AWG and larger are sized under 314.28.
distractorExplanations.b: Swaps the multipliers: straight pulls use 8× the largest raceway, while 6× applies to angle and U pulls.
distractorExplanations.c: Chapter 9 Table 1 governs conductor fill inside raceways, not the dimensions of pull or junction boxes.

options.a: Black, red, blue for phases; white neutral
options.b: Brown, orange, yellow for phases; gray neutral
options.c: Black, red, blue for phases; green neutral
options.d: Black, red, orange for phases; white neutral

distractorExplanations.b: Brown-orange-yellow with gray is the common convention for 480Y/277 V systems, not 208Y/120 V.
distractorExplanations.c: Green or bare is reserved for equipment grounding conductors (250.119); the neutral is white or gray.
distractorExplanations.d: Orange marks the high leg of a 4-wire delta system (110.15), not a phase of a 208Y/120 V wye system.

options.a: Use the white wire as the switched return to the light
options.b: Provide grounded conductor to switch location
options.c: Include a neutral at smart switches, while standard toggles are exempt
options.d: Provide the grounded conductor at the light fixture box only

distractorExplanations.a: 200.7(C)(1) allows a re-identified white conductor only as the supply to the switch, never as the switched return.
distractorExplanations.c: 404.2(C) requires the grounded conductor at most switch locations regardless of the switch type installed.
distractorExplanations.d: The neutral at the fixture is not enough; 404.2(C) requires it at the switch location for future electronic controls.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-wi.explanation: This item asks: “Switch loops must”. The matching rule is: Provide grounded conductor to switch location per current NEC dwelling requirements. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. This follows 404.2(C) for current NEC dwelling requirements.

options.a: Be buried at least 6 in. deep if direct-buried under a lawn
options.b: Enter through an unsealed raceway so that any condensation can drain out
options.c: Be protected from physical damage and meet burial depth/raceway rules
options.d: Rise along the wall without protection above the final grade

distractorExplanations.a: 6 in. is the cover for RMC/IMC; direct-buried cables and conductors generally need 24 in. of cover per Table 300.5.
distractorExplanations.b: 300.5(G) requires raceways entering a building from underground to be sealed against moisture and gas migration.
distractorExplanations.d: 300.5(D) requires protection of conductors emerging from grade up to at least 8 ft above finished grade.

options.a: Neutral with two ungrounded conductors on the same phase
options.b: Equipment grounding conductor used as the common neutral
options.c: Neutral with ungrounded conductors on separate breakers without handle ties
options.d: Neutral with opposing ungrounded conductors on different phases

distractorExplanations.a: On the same phase the currents add on the neutral and can overload it; MWBC hots must be on different phases.
distractorExplanations.b: The EGC may not carry normal load current; an MWBC shares a grounded (neutral) conductor, not the EGC.
distractorExplanations.c: 210.4(B) requires simultaneous disconnection of all ungrounded MWBC conductors, typically by handle ties or a multipole breaker.

options.a: Should follow manufacturer specifications
options.b: Should be tight enough by feel, with torque tools optional
options.c: Should follow Table 310.16 values listed by conductor size
options.d: Should use an impact driver set to maximum for consistent results

distractorExplanations.b: Since NEC 2017, 110.14(D) requires an approved calibrated torque tool where a tightening torque is indicated.
distractorExplanations.c: Table 310.16 lists ampacities, not torque values; torque comes from the equipment manufacturer or Annex I.
distractorExplanations.d: Maximum impact torque can strip or damage terminals; the specified value is applied with a calibrated tool.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-wi.explanation: This item asks: “Torque requirements for terminations”. The matching rule is: Should follow manufacturer specifications; 110.14 requires proper tightening. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. 110.14 requires proper tightening, with a calibrated torque tool when a value is specified.

options.a: 8 inches of box and every 3 ft along run (334.30)
options.b: 12 inches of box and every 4.5 ft along run (334.30)
options.c: 18 inches of box and every 6 ft along run (334.30)
options.d: 24 inches of box and every 10 ft along run (334.30)

distractorExplanations.a: The 8 in. figure applies to single-gang boxes without cable clamps (314.17); 334.30 sets 12 in. and 4.5 ft.
distractorExplanations.c: Too far apart: 334.30 requires NM support within 12 in. of each box and at intervals of no more than 4.5 ft.
distractorExplanations.d: 10 ft is the support interval for raceways such as EMT (358.30), not NM cable, which needs 4.5 ft spacing.

options.a: Located anywhere in the building if the service conductors are in conduit
options.b: Installed in a bathroom if it is the nearest point of entrance
options.c: Readily accessible and located per 230.70 near meter/service entrance
options.d: Accessible to the utility only, with a lockable cover required

distractorExplanations.a: 230.70(A)(1) requires the disconnect at the nearest point of entrance of the service conductors, conduit or not.
distractorExplanations.b: 230.70(A)(2) prohibits service disconnecting means in bathrooms even at the nearest point of entrance.
distractorExplanations.d: The service disconnect must be readily accessible to the occupant; utility-only access applies to the meter seal.

options.a: Main breaker size alone, without an Article 220 load calculation
options.b: Table 250.66, based on the grounding electrode conductor size
options.c: Article 430 motor tables, using the largest motor's FLC
options.d: Calculated load per Article 220 and 230.42/230.82 rules

distractorExplanations.a: Service conductors are sized from the Article 220 calculated load per 230.42, not just from the main breaker rating.
distractorExplanations.b: Table 250.66 sizes the grounding electrode conductor from the service conductor size, not the other way around.
distractorExplanations.c: Article 430 sizes motor circuits; a service is sized from the total calculated load under Article 220.

options.a: Rod(s), plate, concrete encased electrode, or metal underground pipe where available
options.b: Metal underground gas piping bonded at the meter as the electrode
options.c: A single rod alone, without testing or a supplemental electrode
options.d: Interior metal water piping located more than 5 ft from where it enters the building

distractorExplanations.b: 250.52(B) prohibits metal underground gas piping from being used as a grounding electrode.
distractorExplanations.c: 250.53(A)(2) requires a supplemental electrode for a single rod unless it is shown to be 25 ohms or less.
distractorExplanations.d: 250.68(C) limits use of interior water piping as a grounding conductor to the first 5 ft from the point of entrance.

options.a: Applies to doors and porches, with operable windows exempt
options.b: Must meet clearances from openings not designed for conductors
options.c: Is set by the utility alone, since NEC clearance rules stop at the meter
options.d: Is governed by the vertical clearances above roofs in 230.24(A)

distractorExplanations.a: 230.9(A) includes windows designed to be opened along with doors, porches, and balconies.
distractorExplanations.c: Overhead service conductors on the premises side of the service point are covered by NEC Article 230 clearances.
distractorExplanations.d: 230.24(A) covers clearance above roofs; clearance from building openings is a separate rule in 230.9.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-se.explanation: This item asks: “Overhead service clearance from windows”. The matching rule is: Must meet 230.24(B) clearances from openings not designed for conductors. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. For windows, doors, and porches the clearance is 3 ft per 230.9(A).

options.a: The service disconnecting means required by 230.70
options.b: Owned and maintained by the utility in every jurisdiction
options.c: Utility/customer demarcation point; not load center unless combined
options.d: The point where service-entrance conductors end and feeders begin

distractorExplanations.a: A meter socket houses the revenue meter and does not open the circuit; the disconnect is separate unless combined.
distractorExplanations.b: Meter socket ownership varies; in many areas the customer furnishes and installs it to utility specifications.
distractorExplanations.d: Service conductors end at the service disconnect/service equipment, which is where feeders begin, not at the meter.

options.a: Lateral is overhead; drop is underground from utility
options.b: Lateral runs from meter to panel; drop runs pole to meter
options.c: Both are customer-owned service-entrance conductors
options.d: Lateral is underground; drop is overhead from utility

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps the terms: a service drop is overhead and a service lateral is underground.
distractorExplanations.b: Meter-to-panel conductors are service-entrance conductors; a lateral is the underground conductor from the utility.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops and laterals run from the utility to the service point; service-entrance conductors are a separate category.

options.a: Be same length, material, size, and termination
options.b: Be 1/0 AWG or larger, in different lengths per phase as needed
options.c: Be the same size per phase, with mixed copper and aluminum permitted
options.d: Be grouped by phase in separate raceways, one phase per raceway

distractorExplanations.b: 1/0 AWG is the minimum size, but each phase's paralleled conductors must be the same length to share current.
distractorExplanations.c: Paralleled conductors in a phase must be the same material as well as the same size, length, and insulation.
distractorExplanations.d: 300.20 requires all phases and the neutral in each raceway to avoid inductive heating of metal raceways.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-se.explanation: This item asks: “Parallel service conductors must”. The matching rule is: Be same length, material, size, and termination per 310.10(H). Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. In NEC 2023 the parallel-conductor rules are in 310.10(G); insulation type must match too.

options.a: Any branch circuit, provided it has its own overcurrent device
options.b: Supply-side connections like certain solar, MGTs per rules
options.c: Only the meter, with no other equipment allowed ahead of the disconnect
options.d: Feeder panelboards sized at 125% of the service conductor ampacity

distractorExplanations.a: 230.82 permits only listed items ahead of the disconnect; general branch circuits connect on the load side.
distractorExplanations.c: 230.82 lists several permitted items such as surge arresters, PV supply-side connections, and meter disconnects.
distractorExplanations.d: Feeder panelboards are fed from the load side of the service disconnect; 230.82 does not permit them ahead of it.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-se.explanation: This item asks: “230.82 lists permitted loads connected to service conductors”. The matching rule is: Supply-side connections like certain solar, MGTs per rules—not all branch loads. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. Branch loads in general may not connect ahead of the service disconnect.

options.a: The full phase current on balanced 3-phase linear loads
options.b: Only current from 240-volt loads such as ranges' heating elements
options.c: Unbalanced current and harmonic return on single-phase and some 3-phase
options.d: No current, since it is bonded to the grounding electrode

distractorExplanations.a: On balanced linear 3-phase loads the phase currents cancel and the neutral carries little or no current.
distractorExplanations.b: Line-to-line 240 V loads draw no neutral current; the neutral carries the unbalanced 120 V load.
distractorExplanations.d: Bonding to the electrode does not stop neutral current; it carries the unbalanced load back to the source.

options.a: 60 amperes for one-family dwellings under 230.79
options.b: The sum of all branch-circuit breaker ratings installed in the panelboard
options.c: The utility transformer rating serving the building
options.d: Calculated load but not less than minimums in 230.79 for dwelling

distractorExplanations.a: 230.79(C) sets 100 A as the minimum for a one-family dwelling service; 60 A applies to other limited cases.
distractorExplanations.b: Services are sized from the Article 220 calculated load with demand factors, not from adding breaker handle ratings.
distractorExplanations.c: The utility transformer size does not set the NEC service rating; the calculated load and 230.79 minimums do.

options.a: Who owns conductors and which code/rules apply beyond point
options.b: Where the main bonding jumper must be installed in the system
options.c: The service disconnect location under 230.70
options.d: The point where the NEC stops and NFPA 70E work rules begin

distractorExplanations.b: The main bonding jumper is installed at the service disconnect, not at the utility service point.
distractorExplanations.c: The disconnect location is set by 230.70 (nearest point of entrance), not by the utility service point.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 70E covers safe work practices, not ownership; the service point separates utility rules from NEC coverage.

options.a: Bonding and grounding per 250.24
options.b: Bonding and grounding per 250.30
options.c: Grounding at the primary side only, per 250.32
options.d: Bonding at both the transformer and the panel per 250.30

distractorExplanations.a: 250.24 covers grounding of service-supplied systems; separately derived systems such as transformers fall under 250.30.
distractorExplanations.c: 250.32 covers buildings supplied by feeders; a transformer secondary is a separately derived system under 250.30.
distractorExplanations.d: 250.30(A)(1) permits the system bonding jumper at one location only; bonding at both creates parallel neutral paths.

options.a: 60 A, the minimum service for any dwelling under 230.79
options.b: 160 A, set as the dwelling maximum by 230.79
options.c: Not standard—services typically 100A-400A
options.d: 200 A, the largest service permitted for a one-family dwelling

distractorExplanations.a: 230.79(C) sets 100 A as the one-family dwelling minimum; 60 A is not the dwelling minimum.
distractorExplanations.b: 230.79 sets minimum service ratings, not maximums, and there is no 'Class 160' dwelling service rule.
distractorExplanations.d: The NEC sets no 200 A ceiling; dwellings may have 320/400 A or larger services when the calculated load requires.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-se.explanation: This item asks: “Class 160 service overcurrent device maximum for dwelling”. The matching rule is: Not standard—services typically 100A-400A; 160A may exist as equipment rating context. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. 160A may appear only as an equipment rating context.

options.a: Requires an emergency disconnect only for services over 400 A
options.b: Requires an emergency disconnect located inside next to the panel
options.c: Applies to multifamily buildings, while one- and two-family homes are exempt
options.d: Requires readily accessible external disconnect

distractorExplanations.a: 230.85 applies to one- and two-family dwelling services regardless of rating, not only above 400 A.
distractorExplanations.b: 230.85 requires the emergency disconnect at a readily accessible outdoor location so first responders can reach it.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the scope: 230.85 targets one- and two-family dwelling units specifically.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-se.explanation: This item asks: “Emergency disconnect for one- and two-family dwellings (230.85)”. The matching rule is: Requires readily accessible external disconnect as of recent NEC cycles. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. This has applied since the 2020 NEC cycle.

options.a: May be required to prevent gas/moisture migration per 300.5(G) and 230.8
options.b: Is needed for overhead service masts but not underground raceways
options.c: May use any foam sealant, since compatibility with insulation is not required
options.d: Is prohibited because sealing traps condensation inside the raceway

distractorExplanations.b: 300.5(G) specifically targets raceways entering from underground, where moisture and gas can migrate inside.
distractorExplanations.c: 300.5(G) requires sealants identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation.
distractorExplanations.d: Sealing is required, not prohibited; it keeps warm moist air and gases from migrating into equipment.

options.a: Available fault current to size the service overcurrent device
options.b: PPE category and approach boundaries for energized work
options.c: Shock voltage limits for selecting rubber insulating gloves
options.d: Which LOTO steps can be skipped for live troubleshooting

distractorExplanations.a: Available fault current comes from a short-circuit study (110.24); arc flash analysis uses it to find incident energy and PPE.
distractorExplanations.c: Glove class selection comes from the shock risk assessment; arc flash analysis sets arc-rated PPE and the arc boundary.
distractorExplanations.d: Arc flash analysis does not waive lockout/tagout; it sets PPE and boundaries when energized work is justified.

options.a: Open the breaker and begin work once the circuit is labeled
options.b: Verify absence of voltage first, then open the disconnect
options.c: De-energize and verify absence of voltage before contact
options.d: Lock the breaker and test with a non-contact tester only

distractorExplanations.a: Opening and labeling is not enough; the circuit must be locked out and tested for absence of voltage before contact.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the order: open and lock out the disconnect first, then verify absence of voltage.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 70E requires an adequately rated contact test instrument; non-contact testers alone are not acceptable verification.

options.a: OSHA glove classes, with Class 00 equal to 500V
options.b: The arc-flash PPE category printed on the handle
options.c: The UL listing number stamped on the jaw
options.d: ASTM/ISO standards for voltage rating (e.g., 1000V)

distractorExplanations.a: Class 00 (500 V) is a rubber insulating glove class under ASTM D120, not a rating system for insulated hand tools.
distractorExplanations.b: PPE categories rate arc-rated clothing; insulated tools carry a voltage rating such as 1000 V per ASTM F1505/IEC 60900.
distractorExplanations.c: A listing number identifies a product, not its insulation rating; tools are rated to 1000 V under ASTM/IEC standards.

options.a: Arc flash incident energy from enclosed switchgear
options.b: Low oxygen, toxic gases, or flammable vapors
options.c: Step and touch potential from grounded vault walls
options.d: Engulfment by loose cable fill and conduit debris

distractorExplanations.a: Arc flash is an electrical hazard, not an atmospheric one; confined-space testing checks oxygen, toxics, and flammables.
distractorExplanations.c: Step and touch potential is a shock hazard; atmospheric hazards are low oxygen, toxic gases, and flammable vapors.
distractorExplanations.d: Engulfment is a physical confined-space hazard, separate from the atmospheric hazards measured before entry.

options.a: Circuit is live, then dead after switching, then live again on restore
options.b: Tester reads dead on two phases, then the third is checked live
options.c: Tester works on known live, confirms dead, then recheck live
options.d: Meter calibration is current before each shift's first test

distractorExplanations.a: Live-dead-live checks the tester, not the circuit's switching history: test on a known live source before and after.
distractorExplanations.b: Every conductor is tested for absence of voltage; the known-live checks are on a separate source before and after.
distractorExplanations.d: Calibration date matters, but live-dead-live proves the tester is working at the moment of the absence-of-voltage test.

options.a: Detecting arcing signatures on the branch circuit
options.b: Detecting current over 30 mA, the equipment-protection trip level
options.c: Sending fault current over the EGC to trip the breaker
options.d: Detecting imbalance between hot and neutral (~5mA trip)

distractorExplanations.a: Recognizing arcing signatures is the AFCI function; a GFCI compares current on the hot and neutral.
distractorExplanations.b: 30 mA is a typical equipment ground-fault protection (GFPE) level; Class A GFCIs for people trip at about 4–6 mA.
distractorExplanations.c: Clearing faults through the EGC is how the breaker protects equipment; a GFCI trips on a small current imbalance.

options.a: Only qualified persons with appropriate PPE may enter
options.b: Unqualified persons may enter if escorted by a qualified person
options.c: Anyone wearing arc-rated clothing may enter
options.d: Qualified persons may enter without shock PPE if work is brief

distractorExplanations.b: The escort allowance applies to the limited approach boundary; unqualified persons may not cross the restricted boundary.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc-rated clothing addresses arc flash; crossing the restricted (shock) boundary requires qualification and shock PPE.
distractorExplanations.d: Inside the restricted approach boundary a qualified person needs shock protection regardless of task duration.

options.a: Follow Article 527 rules, which govern temporary installations
options.b: Meet NEC Article 590 including protection from damage
options.c: Be removed within 180 days of first energizing
options.d: Use GFCI only for 15A receptacles, not 20A or 30A

distractorExplanations.a: Temporary wiring moved from Article 527 to Article 590 in the 2002 NEC; Article 590 is the current rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Construction temporary wiring is removed when construction is complete (590.3); the 90-day limit is for holiday lighting.
distractorExplanations.d: 590.6 requires GFCI protection for 125 V, single-phase 15, 20, and 30 A receptacles on construction sites.

options.a: Aluminum ladders kept at least 3 ft from overhead lines
options.b: Wood ladders that have been painted to seal and protect the side rails
options.c: Non-conductive side rails or maintain clearance from energized parts
options.d: Metal ladders grounded to the panel enclosure before use

distractorExplanations.a: Conductive ladders should not be used near energized parts, and OSHA sets 10 ft minimum clearance for lines up to 50 kV.
distractorExplanations.b: OSHA prohibits opaque coatings on wood ladders because paint can hide cracks and defects.
distractorExplanations.d: Grounding a metal ladder does not make it safe; contact with energized parts still puts the worker in the fault path.

options.a: Low enough that cotton work clothes provide full protection
options.b: Limited to shock risk, since 480V does not sustain arcs
options.c: Dangerous only at 13.8 kV and above, not 480V
options.d: Severe enough to require arc-rated suit and face shield

distractorExplanations.a: 480 V switchgear incident energy often exceeds what untreated cotton can withstand; arc-rated PPE is required.
distractorExplanations.b: 480 V systems readily sustain arcing faults; arc flash risk is a major hazard at this voltage.
distractorExplanations.c: Many serious arc flash injuries occur on 480 V equipment; severity depends on fault current and clearing time.

options.a: Current passed through body causing tissue damage
options.b: Surface burns only, with no internal injury beneath the skin
options.c: Arc flash thermal burns without current passing through the body
options.d: Static discharge from clothing during the contact

distractorExplanations.b: Entry and exit wounds often hide far more extensive internal tissue, nerve, and cardiac damage along the current path.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc flash causes thermal burns without entry/exit wounds; entry and exit points indicate current flowed through the body.
distractorExplanations.d: Static discharge does not produce entry and exit burns; those mark the current path through the body.

options.a: Store spare parts in the working space if aisles stay open
options.b: Keep combustibles out of working space and equipment area
options.c: Use the dedicated space above panels for storing ladders
options.d: Keep the room locked, with working space clearance optional

distractorExplanations.a: 110.26(B) prohibits using required working space for storage, even if a walkway remains.
distractorExplanations.c: Dedicated equipment space above panelboards must stay clear and cannot be used for storage.
distractorExplanations.d: Locking the room does not waive 110.26 working space; clearances must be maintained at all times.

options.a: Non-contact voltage tester swept near each conductor
options.b: Opening the breaker and checking the panel schedule
options.c: Properly rated test instrument contacting all conductors
options.d: Test instrument on one phase-to-ground pair only

distractorExplanations.a: Non-contact testers can miss shielded or low-level voltage; NFPA 70E requires an adequately rated contact test instrument.
distractorExplanations.b: Panel schedules can be wrong; absence of voltage must be verified by testing, not by documentation.
distractorExplanations.d: Each conductor must be tested phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground; testing one pair can miss a live conductor.

options.a: One who holds a state journeyman license for the work being done
options.b: One who has completed OSHA 10 training on electrical hazards
options.c: One who has experience operating the equipment, without safety training
options.d: One who has skills and knowledge related to construction and operation

distractorExplanations.a: The Article 100 definition is based on skills, knowledge, and safety training, not on holding a license.
distractorExplanations.b: OSHA 10 is general awareness training; qualification requires equipment-specific skills and hazard training.
distractorExplanations.c: Experience alone is not enough; the definition requires safety training to recognize and avoid the hazards.

electrical-journeyman-readiness-check-sa.explanation: This item asks: “Qualified person per NEC means:”. The matching rule is: One who has skills and knowledge related to construction and operation for safety. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. The definition also requires safety training to recognize and avoid the hazards involved.
